definition: In computer science and operations research, exact algorithms are algorithms that always solve an optimization problem to optimality.
details: Unless P = NP, an exact algorithm for an NP-hard optimization problem cannot run in worst-case polynomial time. There has been extensive research on finding exact algorithms whose running time is exponential with a low base.

explainer.lead: An exact algorithm is a guaranteed way to find the best possible answer to an optimization problem, not merely a good approximation. That certainty can come at a high computational cost, especially for NP-hard problems.

tiers.eli5: Imagine trying every allowed way to pack a bag so you can be certain nothing better was missed. An exact algorithm promises to find the very best answer, but for some hard problems that promise can take a very long time to keep.
tiers.practitioner: Use an exact algorithm when a solution must be certified optimal rather than merely good enough. The main pitfall is running time: unless P = NP, an NP-hard optimization problem has no exact algorithm with worst-case polynomial running time. Practical exact methods therefore focus on keeping the exponential running-time base low.
tiers.paperLevel: An exact algorithm for an optimization problem always returns a solution attaining the optimal objective value. If the problem is NP-hard, worst-case polynomial time is impossible unless P = NP. A major research direction is designing exact algorithms with exponential running time and a low base.

explainer.example: Suppose a bag holds at most 4 kg. Item A weighs 4 kg and is worth 6 points; item B weighs 3 kg and is worth 5 points. The feasible choices are empty, A alone, or B alone, so an exact algorithm returns A with value 6 and rules out every better choice.

explainer.goal: Find a feasible solution whose objective value is provably the best possible.
steps: Search without losing any possible optimum.
tradeoffs: NP-hard cases can require exponential time.
Lower exponential bases improve running time.
Speed depends on worst-case problem difficulty.
